solution:
The basic theme of organisation is **classification** — arranging a very large number of elements so that their chemistry can be studied systematically instead of element by element.

The elements are arranged in order of increasing **atomic number**, and elements having similar outer (valence shell) electronic configurations are placed in the same vertical column. Because the properties of an element are governed by its valence shell configuration, elements in one column then show similar physical and chemical properties.

The purpose of this organisation is twofold: it rationalises the known chemical facts about the elements, and it allows the properties of elements not yet studied (or not yet discovered) to be predicted.

Mendeleev used the **atomic weight** (relative atomic mass) of the elements. His Periodic Law states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

**No, he did not stick to it strictly.** His primary aim was to keep elements of similar properties in the same group, so wherever the atomic-weight order conflicted with that aim he set the order aside, arguing that the atomic-weight measurements of the day might be incorrect. The standard example is iodine: although it has a **lower** atomic weight than tellurium (Group VI), Mendeleev placed iodine in Group VII along with fluorine, chlorine and bromine because of its similarity in properties.

He also left **gaps** in the table for elements he believed were still undiscovered (Eka-aluminium and Eka-silicon, later found to be gallium and germanium), rather than filling those places with the next element by atomic weight.

The difference lies in the **property taken as the basis of classification**.

**Mendeleev's Periodic Law:** the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their **atomic weights**.

**Modern Periodic Law:** the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their **atomic numbers**.

In approach, Mendeleev's law was empirical — atomic weight was the only quantitative property then available, and it failed wherever the weight order and the property order disagreed (iodine and tellurium), forcing him to break his own rule.

The modern law rests on the atomic number, which Moseley showed (from the characteristic \(X\)-ray spectra, where a plot of \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against \(Z\) is a straight line while \(\sqrt{\nu}\) against atomic mass is not) to be the more fundamental property of an element. Atomic number equals the nuclear charge and the number of electrons in a neutral atom, so the modern law is essentially a consequence of the periodic variation in **electronic configuration**, which is what actually determines the properties. The anomalies of Mendeleev's arrangement disappear automatically.

The number of elements in a period equals the number of electrons that can be accommodated in the orbitals being filled in that period.

For the sixth period the successive electrons enter the \(6s\), \(4f\), \(5d\) and \(6p\) orbitals, in that order of increasing energy. Counting the orbitals available:

\(6s\): 1 orbital
\(4f\) \((l = 3)\): 7 orbitals
\(5d\) \((l = 2)\): 5 orbitals
\(6p\) \((l = 1)\): 3 orbitals

Total number of orbitals \(= 1 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 16\).

Each orbital accommodates a maximum of 2 electrons, so the maximum number of electrons that can be filled in the sixth period is \(16 \times 2 = 32\).

Since one new element is generated for each electron added, the sixth period has **32 elements**.

Write the electronic configuration by filling orbitals in order of increasing energy after the noble gas radon \((Z = 86)\):

\([\text{Rn}]\,5f^{14}\,6d^{10}\,7s^2\,7p^2\)

Check: \(86 + 14 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 114\).

**Period:** the period number is the highest principal quantum number of the valence shell. Here the outermost shell is \(n = 7\), so the element lies in the **7th period**.

**Group:** the outermost configuration is \(ns^2np^2\), which is the configuration of the carbon family. So the element belongs to **Group 14**, and it is a \(p\)-block element.

Third period means the valence shell is \(n = 3\). The seventeenth group is a \(p\)-block group whose outermost configuration is \(ns^2np^5\).

So the element has the configuration

\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^5\)

Adding the electrons: \(2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17\).

The **atomic number is 17** (the element is chlorine).

A permanent name may pay tribute to a notable scientist, or reflect the place where the element was discovered.

**(ii) Seaborg's group** — element 106, named **Seaborgium (Sg)**. The chapter states this directly: Glenn T. Seaborg's work on the transuranium elements led to the reconfiguration of the periodic table, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1951, and element 106 has been named Seaborgium in his honour.

**(i) Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory** — **Lawrencium (Lr, \(Z = 103\))**, which the chapter lists in Table 3.5, and also **Berkelium (Bk, \(Z = 97\))**; both names come from the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory (after E. O. Lawrence and the city of Berkeley).

[Note: the chapter itself does not say which laboratory named which element for part (i). It gives only the general rule that a name may honour a scientist or a place, and it lists Lawrencium in Table 3.5; the attribution to the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory is read from the element's name and is not stated in this chapter.]

The elements in a vertical column of the periodic table constitute a group or family, and they are placed there precisely because they have the **same number and the same distribution of electrons in their outermost orbitals** — that is, the same valence shell electronic configuration.

For example, all the Group 1 elements have an \(ns^1\) valence shell configuration:
Li \([\text{He}]2s^1\), Na \([\text{Ne}]3s^1\), K \([\text{Ar}]4s^1\), Rb \([\text{Kr}]5s^1\), Cs \([\text{Xe}]6s^1\), Fr \([\text{Rn}]7s^1\).

Chemical properties are decided by the valence electrons — how readily they are lost or gained, and in what number. Since the members of a group all present the same valence shell arrangement to a reacting species, they behave chemically in the same way (all the Group 1 metals lose one electron to form \(\text{M}^+\)) and their physical properties vary regularly rather than randomly.

Hence the properties of an element have a periodic dependence on its atomic number, not on its relative atomic mass.

**Atomic radius.** An atom has no sharp boundary — the electron cloud surrounding it simply fades out — so there is no practical way of measuring the size of an individual atom directly. What is measured is the distance between atoms in the **combined** state, and half of it is taken as the radius:

- **Covalent radius** (for a non-metal): half the internuclear distance between two like atoms joined by a single bond. In \(\text{Cl}_2\) the bond distance is \(198\,\text{pm}\), so the atomic radius of chlorine is \(99\,\text{pm}\).
- **Metallic radius** (for a metal): half the internuclear distance separating the metal cores in the metallic crystal. Adjacent copper atoms in solid copper are \(256\,\text{pm}\) apart, so the metallic radius of copper is \(128\,\text{pm}\).

"Atomic radius" is used for either, depending on whether the element is a non-metal or a metal.

**Ionic radius.** The radius of an ion, estimated by measuring the distances between cations and anions in ionic crystals. A **cation** is smaller than its parent atom (it has fewer electrons but the same nuclear charge); an **anion** is larger than its parent atom (the added electron increases electron-electron repulsion and lowers the effective nuclear charge). For example the ionic radius of \(\text{F}^-\) is \(136\,\text{pm}\) against an atomic radius of \(64\,\text{pm}\) for fluorine, while \(\text{Na}^+\) is \(95\,\text{pm}\) against \(186\,\text{pm}\) for sodium.

So neither quantity is the radius of a free atom; both are operational sizes obtained from the atom or ion in a bonded environment.

**Across a period (left to right): the atomic radius DECREASES.**
Second period: Li \(152\), Be \(111\), B \(88\), C \(77\), N \(74\), O \(66\), F \(64\,\text{pm}\).

Explanation: within a period the electrons are being added to the **same** valence shell, so the shielding by inner electrons hardly changes, while the nuclear charge increases by one unit at each step. The effective nuclear charge experienced by the valence electrons therefore increases, they are pulled in more strongly, and the atom contracts.

**Down a group: the atomic radius INCREASES.**
Group 1: Li \(152\), Na \(186\), K \(231\), Rb \(244\), Cs \(262\,\text{pm}\).

Explanation: on descending a group the principal quantum number \(n\) of the valence shell increases, so the valence electrons occupy a shell that is farther from the nucleus. In addition each new period adds a completely filled inner shell, and these inner electrons shield the valence electrons from the pull of the nucleus. Both effects work the same way, so the size increases regularly.

(Noble gases are excluded from such comparisons: being monoatomic they have no covalent radius, and their non-bonded van der Waals radii are much larger.)

**Isoelectronic species** are atoms and ions that contain the **same number of electrons**. Their radii are nevertheless different, because their nuclear charges differ: the greater the nuclear charge, the more tightly the same electron cloud is held and the smaller the species.

(i) \(\text{F}^-\) has \(9 + 1 = 10\) electrons — isoelectronic with \(\text{Ne}\) (also \(\text{O}^{2-}\), \(\text{N}^{3-}\), \(\text{Na}^+\), \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\text{Al}^{3+}\)).

(ii) \(\text{Ar}\) has 18 electrons — isoelectronic with \(\text{K}^+\) (also \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), \(\text{Cl}^-\), \(\text{S}^{2-}\)).

(iii) \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) has \(12 - 2 = 10\) electrons — isoelectronic with \(\text{Ne}\) (also \(\text{Na}^+\), \(\text{F}^-\), \(\text{O}^{2-}\)).

(iv) \(\text{Rb}^+\) has \(37 - 1 = 36\) electrons — isoelectronic with \(\text{Kr}\) (also \(\text{Sr}^{2+}\), \(\text{Br}^-\)).

**(a) What is common in them.**
Count the electrons:
\(\text{N}^{3-}: 7 + 3 = 10\); \(\text{O}^{2-}: 8 + 2 = 10\); \(\text{F}^-: 9 + 1 = 10\); \(\text{Na}^+: 11 - 1 = 10\); \(\text{Mg}^{2+}: 12 - 2 = 10\); \(\text{Al}^{3+}: 13 - 3 = 10\).

All six species have **10 electrons** — they are **isoelectronic**, each having the electronic configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) of neon.

**(b) Increasing order of ionic radii.**
Since the electron count is the same for all six, the size is decided entirely by the nuclear charge: the larger the positive nuclear charge, the more strongly the ten electrons are pulled in and the smaller the ion.

Nuclear charges: \(\text{N}\,7 < \text{O}\,8 < \text{F}\,9 < \text{Na}\,11 < \text{Mg}\,12 < \text{Al}\,13\).

So the radii run in the reverse order:

\(\text{Al}^{3+} < \text{Mg}^{2+} < \text{Na}^+ < \text{F}^- < \text{O}^{2-} < \text{N}^{3-}\)

**A cation is smaller than its parent atom.** Forming a cation removes one or more electrons while the nuclear charge stays exactly the same. The remaining electrons therefore share the same nuclear pull among fewer of themselves, so each is held more tightly and the electron cloud contracts. Very often the electron removed is the only one in the outermost shell, so the whole valence shell disappears and the ion is left with a smaller inner shell as its outermost one: sodium has an atomic radius of \(186\,\text{pm}\) but \(\text{Na}^+\) has an ionic radius of only \(95\,\text{pm}\).

**An anion is larger than its parent atom.** Adding one or more electrons leaves the nuclear charge unchanged but increases the number of electrons. This increases the electron-electron repulsion in the valence shell and decreases the **effective nuclear charge** felt by each electron, so the electron cloud expands: fluorine has an atomic radius of \(64\,\text{pm}\) whereas \(\text{F}^-\) has an ionic radius of \(136\,\text{pm}\).

Both terms are there to fix a **standard reference state**, so that the values quoted for different elements are measurements of the same thing and can legitimately be compared.

**'Isolated gaseous atom'** — the atom must be free from the influence of any neighbouring atom, ion or molecule. In a liquid or a solid, or even in a gas at high pressure, the electron being removed (or added) also feels the attraction and repulsion of the surrounding particles, so the energy measured would include those interactions and would depend on the state and the surroundings rather than on the atom alone. The gaseous, isolated atom is the only condition in which the energy belongs to that atom by itself.

**'Ground state'** — the atom must be in its lowest energy electronic state. An excited atom already holds extra energy and has its electron in a higher orbital, so less energy would be needed to remove it; the value obtained would depend on which excited state the atom happened to be in.

Without both conditions the numbers would not be reproducible, and the periodic trends in ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy could not be drawn from them.

The ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove the electron from the isolated gaseous atom in its ground state, i.e. to take the electron from its ground-state energy up to zero energy (free electron at rest):

\(\text{H(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}^+\text{(g)} + e^-\)

Energy required per atom \(= 0 - (-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}) = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\).

For one mole of hydrogen atoms, multiply by the Avogadro constant \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\):

\(\Delta_i H = (2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1})\)

\(\Delta_i H = 13.13 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 1.31 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

Ionization enthalpy of atomic hydrogen \(= 1.31 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\) (that is, about \(1312\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

**(i) Be has a higher \(\Delta_i H\) than B** (Be \(899\), B \(801\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)), even though boron has the greater nuclear charge.

The reason is **which orbital the electron comes out of**. Beryllium is \(1s^2 2s^2\), so the electron removed is a \(2s\) electron. Boron is \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\), so the electron removed is a \(2p\) electron. Within the same principal quantum level an \(s\)-electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than a \(p\)-electron and is attracted more strongly; conversely the \(2p\) electron of boron is more effectively shielded from the nucleus by the inner core **and** by the \(2s\) electrons. It is therefore easier to remove the \(2p\) electron of boron than the \(2s\) electron of beryllium, and boron has the smaller first ionization enthalpy.

**(ii) O has a lower \(\Delta_i H\) than N** (N \(1402\), O \(1314\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Nitrogen is \(2s^2 2p^3\): by Hund's rule its three \(2p\) electrons occupy three different \(2p\) orbitals, singly. Oxygen is \(2s^2 2p^4\): two of its four \(2p\) electrons must share the same \(2p\) orbital, which produces extra electron-electron repulsion. That repulsion helps push the fourth \(2p\) electron out, so removing it from oxygen takes less energy than removing one of the three unpaired \(2p\) electrons from nitrogen.

**O has a lower \(\Delta_i H\) than F** (F \(1681\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)) for the ordinary across-a-period reason: fluorine has one more proton than oxygen with the electron still entering the same \(n = 2\) shell, so the effective nuclear charge is larger, the valence electrons are held more tightly, and the ionization enthalpy is higher. In fluorine no additional pairing penalty is introduced relative to oxygen — the pairing has already begun at oxygen.

The two comparisons involve removing electrons from quite different environments.

**First ionization enthalpy: Na \(<\) Mg.**
Na is \([\text{Ne}]3s^1\) and Mg is \([\text{Ne}]3s^2\). Both lose a \(3s\) electron, but magnesium has one more proton and its \(3s\) electrons feel a higher effective nuclear charge, being in the same shell with essentially the same shielding. The \(3s\) electron of magnesium is therefore held more tightly, and

\(\Delta_i H_1(\text{Na}) = 496 < \Delta_i H_1(\text{Mg}) = 737\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

**Second ionization enthalpy: Na \(>\) Mg.**
After the first ionization the two ions are quite different:

\(\text{Na}^+ = [\text{Ne}]\) — a complete, very stable noble gas configuration, with no valence electron left.
\(\text{Mg}^+ = [\text{Ne}]3s^1\) — still one loosely held valence electron outside the noble gas core.

Removing the second electron from \(\text{Na}^+\) means breaking into the stable, tightly bound neon core, where the electron is much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded. Removing the second electron from \(\text{Mg}^+\) only takes the remaining \(3s\) valence electron. The energy required in the first case is therefore very much greater, so the second ionization enthalpy of sodium is higher than that of magnesium.

This is the general rule that the greatest jump in ionization enthalpy comes when an electron has to be taken out of a core noble gas configuration.

Down a group the nuclear charge actually **increases**, which by itself would raise the ionization enthalpy. It falls instead because two other factors act in the opposite direction and together outweigh it:

**1. Increasing atomic size (increasing \(n\)).** On descending a group the valence electrons occupy a shell of higher principal quantum number and are therefore, on average, increasingly farther from the nucleus. The electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron weakens with distance, so less energy is needed to pull it away. (Group 1 atomic radii: Li \(152\), Na \(186\), K \(231\), Rb \(244\), Cs \(262\,\text{pm}\).)

**2. Increasing shielding (screening) by the inner electrons.** Each new period adds a completely filled inner shell between the nucleus and the valence electron. Shielding is most effective when the inner shells are completely filled, which is exactly the situation in the alkali metals, where a single outermost \(ns\) electron sits outside a noble gas core. The valence electron therefore experiences an **effective** nuclear charge much smaller than the actual nuclear charge, and this screening grows down the group.

Because the increase in shielding (together with the increase in distance) outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, the outermost electron is progressively easier to remove and \(\Delta_i H\) decreases: Li \(520\), Na \(496\), K \(419\), Rb \(403\), Cs \(374\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

The general trend is that ionization enthalpy decreases steadily down a group. Group 13 obeys it only from B to Al:

B \(801\) \(\rightarrow\) Al \(577\) — a large fall, as expected (size increases, shielding increases).

Al \(577\) \(\rightarrow\) Ga \(579\) — a slight **rise** instead of a fall.
In \(558\) \(\rightarrow\) Tl \(589\) — again a rise.

The cause is the **kind of inner electrons added** between one member and the next, and how badly they shield.

Between Al and Ga a whole \(3d^{10}\) set is filled for the first time. Shielding is effective when the intervening orbitals are spherically symmetric and lie well inside — this is true of filled \(s\) and \(p\) shells, but \(d\) electrons are poor screeners. The ten \(3d\) electrons therefore fail to compensate for the ten extra protons, so the \(4p\) valence electron of gallium feels a **larger** effective nuclear charge than the \(3p\) electron of aluminium. The expected drop is cancelled, and \(\Delta_i H\) even rises slightly.

Between In and Tl the same thing happens more strongly: fourteen \(4f\) electrons are added in addition to ten \(5d\) electrons, and \(f\) electrons shield even more poorly than \(d\) electrons. The resulting increase in effective nuclear charge (and the accompanying contraction in size) raises the ionization enthalpy of thallium above that of indium.

So the deviation is not a failure of the size argument — it is that the increase in nuclear charge is not matched by an equal increase in shielding, because the intervening electrons are \(d\) and \(f\) electrons.

[Note: this chapter teaches the shielding argument itself (that screening is effective only when the inner orbitals are completely filled, and that the trend depends on shielding versus nuclear charge) but explicitly defers the detailed treatment of the \(d\)-block contraction and the lanthanoid contraction to the later group-wise units. The step from 'poor shielding by \(d\) and \(f\) electrons' onward is therefore an application of the chapter's own principle rather than a statement printed in it.]

**(i) O or F — fluorine has the more negative electron gain enthalpy.**
Both belong to the second period, and electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative as one moves left to right across a period, because the effective nuclear charge increases and the atom is smaller, so the incoming electron is added closer to the nucleus. Fluorine also needs only one electron to reach the stable \(2s^2 2p^6\) noble gas configuration. From Table 3.7: O \(-141\), F \(-328\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

**(ii) F or Cl — chlorine has the more negative electron gain enthalpy.**
This is the well-known exception to the down-a-group trend. Fluorine is a very small atom and the incoming electron has to enter the compact \(n = 2\) shell, where it suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already crowded into that small region. In chlorine the electron enters the larger \(n = 3\) shell, which offers a bigger region of space, so the electron-electron repulsion is much less. The gain in stability is therefore greater for chlorine. From Table 3.7: F \(-328\), Cl \(-349\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

So the answers are **F** in (i) and **Cl** in (ii).

The second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is expected to be **positive**.

The first step,

\(\text{O(g)} + e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^-\text{(g)}\),

adds an electron to a **neutral** atom. The nucleus attracts the incoming electron, energy is released, and \(\Delta_{eg}H_1\) is negative (\(-141\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

The second step,

\(\text{O}^-\text{(g)} + e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\text{(g)}\),

adds an electron to a species that is **already negatively charged**. The incoming electron is now repelled by the net negative charge of \(\text{O}^-\), and it must in addition be forced into a \(2p\) orbital that is already occupied, adding further electron-electron repulsion in a small \(n = 2\) shell. Work has to be **done on** the system to push the second electron in, so the process is endothermic.

Hence the second electron gain enthalpy is positive — not merely less negative than the first, but of the opposite sign. (This is why \(\text{O}^{2-}\) is not formed in the gas phase spontaneously; it exists in ionic solids only because the lattice energy released more than pays for it.)

**Electron gain enthalpy \((\Delta_{eg}H)\)** is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an **isolated gaseous atom** in its ground state to convert it into a gaseous negative ion:

\(\text{X(g)} + e^- \rightarrow \text{X}^-\text{(g)}\)

It is a property of the **free atom**, it is an experimentally measurable energy with units of \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and it has a definite sign (negative when energy is released, positive when energy must be supplied, as for the noble gases). It measures the ease with which a **lone** atom accepts a **complete extra** electron.

**Electronegativity** is a qualitative measure of the ability of an atom **in a chemical compound** to attract the **shared** electrons of a bond towards itself. It refers to an atom that is already bonded, not to a free atom; it concerns a *shared* electron pair being pulled, not an electron being wholly captured; it is **not a measurable quantity** and has no units, being expressed only on arbitrary scales (Pauling, Mulliken-Jaffe, Allred-Rochow), with fluorine assigned 4.0 on the widely used Pauling scale; and it is **not constant** for an element — it varies with the element to which the atom is bound.

The two do run parallel (both increase across a period and decrease down a group), which is why electron gain enthalpy is sometimes used as a guide to electronegativity, but they are different properties of different situations.

The statement is **not correct**.

Electronegativity is not a property an atom carries around unchanged. It is the ability of an atom **in a chemical compound** to attract the shared electrons of a bond towards itself, and that ability depends on the environment the atom finds itself in — in particular on the atom to which it is bonded, and also on its oxidation state and hybridisation. The chapter states this explicitly: the electronegativity of any given element is not constant, it varies depending on the element to which it is bound.

The value 3.0 quoted for nitrogen is an **approximate, average** value on the Pauling scale, of the kind listed in Table 3.8(a). It is useful for comparing nitrogen with other elements and for predicting trends, but it is not a fixed constant reproduced exactly in every nitrogen compound. Electronegativity is in any case not a measurable quantity, which is why several different scales (Pauling, Mulliken-Jaffe, Allred-Rochow) exist and give somewhat different numbers.

So one should react by saying that 3.0 is a representative Pauling-scale value for nitrogen, not a constant valid for all nitrogen compounds.

**(a) As the atom gains an electron — it becomes an anion, and the radius INCREASES.**
The number of protons in the nucleus is unchanged, but there is now one extra electron in the valence shell. This increases the electron-electron repulsion among the valence electrons, and it decreases the **effective nuclear charge** experienced by each of them (the same nuclear pull is now shared by more electrons). The net repulsion outweighs the nuclear attraction, the electron cloud expands, and the ion is larger than the parent atom. Example: fluorine \(64\,\text{pm}\), \(\text{F}^-\) \(136\,\text{pm}\).

**(b) As the atom loses an electron — it becomes a cation, and the radius DECREASES.**
Again the nuclear charge is unchanged, but there are now fewer electrons to share it, so each remaining electron experiences a larger effective nuclear charge and is drawn in more tightly. In addition, for a representative metal the electron lost is usually the only electron in the outermost shell, so that shell vanishes altogether and the next inner (smaller) shell becomes the outermost one. Example: sodium \(186\,\text{pm}\), \(\text{Na}^+\) \(95\,\text{pm}\).

The general rule that follows: for ions of the same charge type, and for isoelectronic species, size is decided by the balance between nuclear charge and electron-electron repulsion — a greater positive charge gives a smaller ion, a greater negative charge a larger one.

The first ionization enthalpies of two isotopes of the same element are expected to be the **same**.

Ionization enthalpy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. That energy is fixed by how strongly the electron is held, which depends on

- the **nuclear charge** \((Z)\), and
- the **electronic configuration** — how far the electron is from the nucleus and how well it is shielded by the inner electrons.

Isotopes of an element differ only in the **number of neutrons** in the nucleus. They have the same atomic number, hence the same nuclear charge, the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration. Neutrons are uncharged, so they exert no electrostatic force on the electrons, and the electron being removed is in an identical environment in both isotopes.

The isotopes differ in mass, but mass does not enter the electrostatic attraction that has to be overcome. This is exactly the sense in which the Modern Periodic Law is stated in terms of atomic number rather than atomic mass: properties are periodic functions of \(Z\).

So the two isotopes have the same first ionization enthalpy. (Only an extremely small difference arises from the change in reduced mass of the nucleus-electron system, which is negligible for all elements heavier than hydrogen and is not considered at this level.)

| Property | Metals | Non-metals |
|---|---|---|
| Position in the Periodic Table | left side | top right-hand side |
| Abundance | more than 78% of all known elements | fewer than about twenty elements |
| Physical state at room temperature | usually solids (mercury is liquid; gallium and caesium melt at \(303\,\text{K}\) and \(302\,\text{K}\)) | usually solids or gases (boron and carbon are exceptions among the solids, having high melting points) |
| Melting and boiling points | usually high | usually low |
| Conduction of heat and electricity | good conductors | poor conductors |
| Mechanical behaviour | malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires) | most non-metallic solids are brittle, neither malleable nor ductile |
| Ionization enthalpy | low — they lose electrons readily | high — they do not lose electrons readily |
| Electron gain enthalpy | small or positive | large and negative; they readily accept electrons |
| Electronegativity | low | high |
| Ions formed | cations, by loss of electrons | anions, by gain of electrons |
| Nature of the normal oxide | basic (e.g. \(\text{Na}_2\text{O}\)) | acidic (e.g. \(\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7\)) |

The change from metallic to non-metallic character across a row is **not abrupt**: it is marked by the thick zig-zag line running diagonally across the Periodic Table. Elements bordering that line — silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium — show properties characteristic of both classes and are called **metalloids** or **semi-metals**.

The trends: metallic character increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period; non-metallic character does the opposite.

**(a) An element with five electrons in the outer subshell.**
Five electrons in the outermost \(p\) subshell means the configuration \(ns^2np^5\), which is the halogen family, Group 17. Example: **fluorine**, \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^5\) (chlorine, \([\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^5\), serves equally well).

**(b) An element that would tend to lose two electrons.**
An element with two electrons in its outermost shell, \(ns^2\), loses both to reach a stable noble gas configuration. These are the alkaline earth metals of Group 2, which have low ionization enthalpies and readily form \(\text{M}^{2+}\). Example: **magnesium**, \([\text{Ne}]3s^2\) (or calcium).

**(c) An element that would tend to gain two electrons.**
An element two electrons short of a noble gas configuration, \(ns^2np^4\) — the chalcogens of Group 16, which have highly negative electron gain enthalpies and readily add two electrons to form \(\text{X}^{2-}\). Example: **oxygen**, \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^4\) (or sulphur).

**(d) The group having metal, non-metal, liquid as well as gas at room temperature.**
**Group 17**, the halogens. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid non-metal, and since metallic character increases as one goes down a group, astatine at the bottom of the group is the member showing metallic character.

[Note: the chapter does not print the physical states of the halogens anywhere, and it does not call astatine a metal. What it does give is the trend used above — that within the \(p\)-block the metallic character increases down a group — and the fact that the halogens are Group 17. The identification of which halogen is a gas, which a liquid and which the metallic one is therefore brought in from outside this chapter. Group 1 is worth ruling out explicitly: it does contain hydrogen (a non-metal gas) and metals, and the chapter notes that caesium melts at \(302\,\text{K}\) — but \(302\,\text{K}\) is \(29\,^\circ\text{C}\), so caesium is still a solid at ordinary room temperature and Group 1 supplies no liquid.]

The two groups sit at opposite extremes of a period, and their chemical reactivity is measured by opposite processes — so the same underlying trend in size produces opposite orders.

**Group 1 (alkali metals): reactivity is shown by the LOSS of an electron.**
An alkali metal reacts by giving up its single \(ns^1\) electron to form \(\text{M}^+\). The easier that electron is to remove, the more reactive the metal. Down the group the atomic radius increases (Li \(152 \rightarrow\) Cs \(262\,\text{pm}\)) and the shielding of the nuclear charge by the filled inner shells increases; this outweighs the rise in nuclear charge, so the ionization enthalpy falls steadily:

Li \(520\), Na \(496\), K \(419\), Rb \(403\), Cs \(374\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

The outermost electron is therefore progressively easier to lose, and reactivity **increases** down the group: Li \(<\) Na \(<\) K \(<\) Rb \(<\) Cs.

**Group 17 (halogens): reactivity is shown by the GAIN of an electron.**
A halogen reacts by accepting one electron into its \(ns^2np^5\) shell to form \(\text{X}^-\). The more strongly the atom attracts that electron, the more reactive it is. Down the group the atom gets larger, the incoming electron is added farther from the nucleus and is more shielded, so the pull on it weakens. Electronegativity falls accordingly:

F \(4.0\), Cl \(3.0\), Br \(2.8\), I \(2.5\), At \(2.2\).

So the tendency to gain an electron, and hence the reactivity, **decreases** down the group: F \(>\) Cl \(>\) Br \(>\) I.

**A point worth noting.** Judged by electron gain enthalpy alone the order would start wrongly, because chlorine \((-349\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1})\) has a *more* negative value than fluorine \((-328\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1})\). That is the exception explained in the chapter: fluorine is so small that the incoming electron must enter the compact \(n = 2\) shell and suffers significant repulsion from the electrons already there. Fluorine's overall reactivity is nevertheless the highest, which is why the size/electronegativity argument, and not the electron gain enthalpy of the single step, gives the correct order.

The block to which an element belongs is decided by the type of atomic orbital that receives the last electron.

**\(s\)-Block** — Groups 1 and 2 (alkali metals and alkaline earth metals):
\(ns^{1-2}\)

**\(p\)-Block** — Groups 13 to 18:
\(ns^2np^{1-6}\)
(the configuration runs from \(ns^2np^1\) at the start of each period's \(p\)-block to \(ns^2np^6\) at the noble gas which closes it)

**\(d\)-Block** — Groups 3 to 12, the transition elements:
\((n-1)d^{1-10}\,ns^{0-2}\)

**\(f\)-Block** — the lanthanoids and actinoids, the inner-transition elements:
\((n-2)f^{1-14}\,(n-1)d^{0-1}\,ns^2\)

Here \(n\) is the principal quantum number of the outermost shell, which is also the period number.

In each case the period number is \(n\), the outermost principal quantum number; the block follows from the subshell receiving the last electron; and the group follows from the number of valence electrons.

**(i) \(ns^2np^4\) for \(n = 3\), i.e. \(3s^2 3p^4\).**
Full configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4\), so \(Z = 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16\) — **sulphur**.
Last electron enters a \(p\) orbital \(\Rightarrow\) \(p\)-block. Six valence electrons in the \(p\)-block \(\Rightarrow\) Group \(12 + 4 = 16\).
**Period 3, Group 16, \(p\)-block** (a chalcogen).

**(ii) \((n-1)d^2ns^2\) for \(n = 4\), i.e. \(3d^2 4s^2\).**
Full configuration \([\text{Ar}]3d^2 4s^2\), so \(Z = 18 + 2 + 2 = 22\) — **titanium**.
Last electron enters a \(d\) orbital \(\Rightarrow\) \(d\)-block. Group number for a \(d\)-block element \(= (\text{number of } (n-1)d \text{ electrons}) + (\text{number of } ns \text{ electrons}) = 2 + 2 = 4\).
**Period 4, Group 4, \(d\)-block** (a transition element).

**(iii) \((n-2)f^7(n-1)d^1ns^2\) for \(n = 6\), i.e. \(4f^7 5d^1 6s^2\).**
Full configuration \([\text{Xe}]4f^7 5d^1 6s^2\), so \(Z = 54 + 7 + 1 + 2 = 64\) — **gadolinium**.
The last electrons are entering an \(f\) subshell \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\)-block, and with \(n = 6\) it is a member of the \(4f\) inner-transition series, the **lanthanoids**.
**Period 6, \(f\)-block (lanthanoid series), placed with Group 3.**

Read the three columns together. A very large jump from \(\Delta_i H_1\) to \(\Delta_i H_2\) shows that the first electron removed emptied the valence shell, so the second must come out of a noble gas core; a very high \(\Delta_i H_1\) together with a **positive** \(\Delta_{eg}H\) marks a noble gas; a highly negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) marks a non-metal.

**Element I** \((520,\ 7300,\ -60)\): a modest first ionization enthalpy followed by a fourteen-fold jump — one valence electron only, an **alkali metal** (Group 1).
**Element II** \((419,\ 3051,\ -48)\): the same pattern with an even lower \(\Delta_i H_1\) — also an **alkali metal**, and lower in the group than I.
**Element III** \((1681,\ 3374,\ -328)\): high \(\Delta_i H_1\) and a strongly negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) — a **halogen**, and the most electron-attracting one here.
**Element IV** \((1008,\ 1846,\ -295)\): also a halogen, but with a lower \(\Delta_i H_1\) and a less negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) — a **halogen lower down the group**.
**Element V** \((2372,\ 5251,\ +48)\): the highest \(\Delta_i H_1\) of all and a **positive** electron gain enthalpy (it will neither lose nor gain an electron) — a **noble gas**.
**Element VI** \((738,\ 1451,\ -40)\): \(\Delta_i H_2\) is only about twice \(\Delta_i H_1\), so a second electron is still available in the valence shell before the core is reached — **two** valence electrons, an **alkaline earth metal** (Group 2).

Answers:

**(a) The least reactive element — V.** It has the largest ionization enthalpy (so it will not lose an electron) and a positive electron gain enthalpy (so it will not gain one); it has a closed, stable shell.

**(b) The most reactive metal — II.** Among the two metals of Group 1 it has the lower first ionization enthalpy \((419 < 520)\), so it loses its valence electron most readily; alkali metal reactivity is shown by loss of an electron.

**(c) The most reactive non-metal — III.** It has the most negative electron gain enthalpy \((-328)\); halogen reactivity is shown by gain of an electron.

**(d) The least reactive non-metal — IV.** Of the two non-metals its electron gain enthalpy is the less negative \((-295)\) and its ionization enthalpy the lower, so it attracts an electron least strongly. (Element V is excluded here, since as a noble gas it is not classed with the reactive non-metals; it is the answer to part (a).)

**(e) The metal forming a stable binary halide \(\text{MX}_2\) — VI.** A halide \(\text{MX}_2\) needs a metal with a valence of two, and VI is the only element here whose second ionization enthalpy is still small enough for both valence electrons to be lost — that is, an alkaline earth metal.

**(f) The metal forming a predominantly stable covalent halide MX — I.** MX requires a metal of valence one, so it is one of the two alkali metals; and of those, I is the higher in the group (its \(\Delta_i H_1\) is larger, \(520\) against \(419\)), hence the smaller atom with the greater polarising power. The chapter states this exception directly: the compounds of the \(s\)-block elements are predominantly ionic **with the exception of those of lithium and beryllium**. So the small alkali metal at the top of Group 1 is the one whose halide is predominantly covalent.

Use the valence of each element, which for a representative element is either the number of electrons in the outermost orbitals or eight minus that number, and combine the two so that the valences balance.

**(a) Lithium and oxygen.** Li is in Group 1, valence 1; O is in Group 16, valence \(8 - 6 = 2\). Formula \(\text{Li}_2\text{O}\).

**(b) Magnesium and nitrogen.** Mg is in Group 2, valence 2; N is in Group 15, valence \(8 - 5 = 3\). Formula \(\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2\).

**(c) Aluminium and iodine.** Al is in Group 13, valence 3; I belongs to the halogen family, valence 1. Formula \(\text{AlI}_3\).

**(d) Silicon and oxygen.** Si is in Group 14, valence 4; O has valence 2. Formula \(\text{SiO}_2\).

**(e) Phosphorus and fluorine.** F is a halogen, valence 1. P is in Group 15, and the periodic trend in valence for that group is 3 or 5 (a Group 15 element can use either \(8 - 5 = 3\) or its 5 valence electrons). Both binary fluorides are therefore predicted: \(\text{PF}_3\) and \(\text{PF}_5\).

**(f) Element 71 and fluorine.** \(Z = 71\) is lutetium, the last member of the lanthanoid series (the lanthanoids run from \(\text{Ce}\ (Z = 58)\) to \(\text{Lu}\ (Z = 71)\)). Its configuration is \([\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^1 6s^2\); the \(4f\) subshell is complete, leaving three electrons \((5d^1 6s^2)\) available for bonding, so the valence is 3. Formula \(\text{LuF}_3\).
